--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.to_undirected()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Convert the graph to an undirected graph. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.to_undirected()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Convert the graph to an undirected graph. title: >- [Graph.to_undirected()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Convert the graph to an undirected graph. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Convert the graph to an undirected graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L48055-L48179){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.to_undirected() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Convert to undirected](../assets/graphs/to-undirected.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A directed graph with a mutual pair of accent arrows between A and B, plus arrows A to D and D to C. After to_undirected(), the mutual pair collapses into a single accent edge A to B, and the other two edges simply lose their arrowheads." width="100%"} Creates a new graph with the same nodes and edges, but without edge direction. If the graph is already undirected, returns a new copy. For directed graphs, converts directed edges to undirected edges, removing duplicate pairs. Many analyses are defined only for undirected graphs (cliques, the leading-eigenvector and other community methods, most clustering measures), and many relationships are better treated as mutual even when the data records a direction. Converting is the usual way to: - run undirected-only algorithms on directed data (e.g., `find_cliques()` or `cmty_l_eigenvec()`) - treat a one-way relation such as "follows", "cites", or "emails" as plain "connected to" - study weak connectivity, where direction does not matter Node IDs, labels, and node attributes are carried over unchanged. Every directed edge becomes an undirected edge with its weight and attributes. When both `A -> B` and `B -> A` exist, only the first one added is kept, so the weight and attributes of the reverse edge are discarded rather than combined. Node and kept edge IDs are the same as in the original. The original graph is not modified. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new undirected Graph with the same nodes and edges (with mutual directed pairs merged into single edges). ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~to_directed`) : Turn each undirected edge into a pair of directed edges. [](`~reciprocity`) : The share of directed edges that are returned. [](`~weakly_connected_components`) : The components when direction is ignored. [](`~remove_duplicate_edges`) : Merge parallel edges. ## Examples {.doc-examples} "Alice" and "Bob" follow each other, so their two directed edges collapse into one undirected connection, and three directed edges become two: ::: {#bd6d3d81 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec followers = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("Alice", "Bob"), ("Bob", "Alice"), ("Bob", "Charlie")], directed=True, ) connections = followers.to_undirected() connections.is_directed(), connections.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (False, ['Alice--Bob', 'Bob--Charlie']) ``` ::: ::: When a mutual pair is merged, the edge added first wins. Here the `A -> B` edge (weight `2.0`) is kept and the `B -> A` edge (weight `5.0`) is dropped: ::: {#e8fcf53c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} weighted = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B", 2.0), ("B", "A", 5.0)], directed=True ) merged = weighted.to_undirected() merged.get_edge_df().select("source", "target", "weight") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Who does business with whom A month of payments between bank accounts has a direction on every edge: who paid whom. Dropping the direction asks a simpler question, which accounts have dealt with each other at all. The 35 payments join 33 pairs of accounts, because Dee and Eve paid each other, and so did Max and Nia: ::: {#2e53a995 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} payments = ec.payments() payments.layout_kamada_kawai(weighted=False) dealings = payments.to_undirected() payments.count_edges(), dealings.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (35, 33) ``` ::: ::: Each of those two pairs keeps the amount of its first payment, Dee's 80 to Eve and Nia's 900 to Max, and loses the other (Eve's 25 back to Dee and Max's 40 to Nia). To keep a total for each pair, add up the amounts before converting: ::: {#3c414013 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl kept = dealings.find_edge_ids("Dee", "Eve") kept += dealings.find_edge_ids("Max", "Nia") rows = dealings.get_edge_df().filter(pl.col("id").is_in(kept)) rows.select("amount", "date") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The layout was computed before converting, and the positions are node attributes, so both views are drawn in the same places. The undirected one has no arrows, and the two pairs are joined by one line each instead of two: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#a8671b7b .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} payments.plot(layout="pos", label_by="label", width=360, height=360) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
